title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin shares their personal journey of discovering meaning and healing through Soto Zen Buddhism, which began with a turning point when they adopted a child with special needs. Through this challenging experience, they found solace and peace through Buddhist practice, learning to accept and cope with their emotions. As they continue on their path, Nyogen emphasizes the transformative power of ritual, such as zazen, in creating sacred space for self-reflection and healing, ultimately revealing the divine significance in all aspects of life.

sentences.text: *What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday, and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
Our life is the creation of our mind.
If a person speaks or acts with an impure mind, suffering follows as the wheel of the cart follows the beast that pulls it.
What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday, and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
If a person speaks or acts with an impure mind, joy follows as the shadow follows the body.
He insulted me, he hurt me, he defeated me, he robbed me.
Those who think such thoughts will not be free of hate, for hate is not conquered by hate.
Hate is conquered by love.
This is the eternal law.*
This verse has ended up meaning a lot to me.
When I first came to Zen, I came to it out of anger.
I had a lot more hatred in my heart than I did have love.
I still feel like it is so surprising that I am here.
It's just so improbable that little Connie Sue Schaefer of Wilmington, Ohio ended up as a Shuso in a Zen Buddhist Sangha in the Pacific Northwest.
How could that possibly have happened?
So many things had to play out in a certain way for me to be sitting here right now.
It's really pretty incredible.

If I hadn't been having problems with my marriage, and my ex-husband and I had not gone to a psychotherapist, a counselor who happened to answer a question in terms of her Zen practice, I would not be here today.
So my thanks always go out to Nancy Welch for the fact that I'm part of this group.
And even from being part of this group, how did I come to be Nogun Seku and how did I come to be Shuso or head student?
It's just so improbable.
So my way seeking mind has been pretty confused.
It's taken quite a few detours.
I even once left the group for about three years because I was upset about some things.
And then I found that I had to return.
I just, for myself, I had to return.
And I found that there has been a pattern in my practice.
It's been a practice of turning toward or turning away.
Before I do anything else, I want to say a couple more thank yous.
Not only to Nancy for the fact that I'm here at all, but also to Tim.
I feel like in some ways we grew up together in the sangha as he was becoming a priest and I was becoming a practitioner for the first time.
So thanks to Tim.
And of course always my thanks to Norman.
I was incredibly fortunate in that the first time I went to an introduction to Zen, it was led by Norman Fischer.
And also fortunate that he didn't turn out to be someone like Jim Jones, because I would have followed him anywhere.
I still think of my practice and my life in terms of chapters.

Some of those have been kind of a strange tale: Fire and Brimstone, Tarzan, Betrayal, Popcorn, Princeton and Publishing, Microsoft, which was a religion unto itself, Not Good Enough, A Kid Who Can't Talk, Can't Talk at All, Anger, Africa, Practice, Shawshank Redemption, Great Blue Herons, Zoketsu, Zazen, Out of the Ashes, Eno, John Deere, Shuso.
So the turning away has been turning away from pain and turning away from difficulty, turning away from reality, and then slowly, gradually through practice, learning that I can turn toward my life.
I can turn toward what's most difficult, at least to some extent, without falling apart.
So I'm going to start with chapter two.
I was probably about 10 years old and reading my very first novel, Tarzan and the Golden Lion.
Tarzan wandered into a decaying temple deep in the African jungle and he caught a whiff of incense, and I was intrigued.

*Intermingled with the spore of the gorilla man was the suggestion of a sweet scent burning incense along with the scent spore of Numa, the lion.* So I turned toward wanting to go to Africa, and I went to Africa.
I think I knew acacia trees before I ever saw one.
In some previous life they must have been part of my life.
It was a wonderful trip.
I also should have paid more attention to the brochure that said that the roads in Tanzania were really bad and you shouldn't go if you have bad problems.
I never had bad problems before but the roads in Tanzania did it to me.

But it also meant that I got flown out of the Serengeti by the Flying Doctor Society, and I was able to look down from the air and see the beginning, the very beginning of the migration of the wildebeest into the Serengeti.
So that was pretty cool.
I would love to go back to Africa.
And I will get to the Zen part, but a little more background.
Fire and brimstone.
There's a flyer on the back table for a revival that was led by Sam Schaefer, my great uncle Sam.
I remember going to some of these revivals, and uncle Sam striding back and forth in a loud voice talking about sin and damnation and abomination in the sight of the Lord.
I don't remember a whole lot more about it except that I liked the music.
*Oh come to the church in the wild.
Oh come to the church in the lane.*
I was very young.
So I attended Sunday school.
I liked Sunday school a lot.
I taught vacation Bible school.
I studied the Bible and I even considered that I might want to become a missionary.
I don't want Chris to hear that.
Then I invited a couple kids from my homeroom.
They weren't close friends, just a couple people that I hung out with in the homeroom, and for some reason, I don't remember why, I invited them to come to church with me.
They came to Sunday school and it was so clear that they were not welcome.
They happened to be black and in my all-white church there was no place for them.
Everyone was excruciatingly polite, I remember, but it was just very clear that they were not welcome there.
I was about 13.
I didn't do anything dramatic.
I didn't blow up at people or even talk about it, but I turned away.
I wish I had said something to people at the time, but I was shy.
I don't know, I didn't have enough courage to confront the hypocrisy.
If I had been older or more mature I might have also realized that I would find the same kind of thing in other religions, but I didn't.
I just felt, yeah, I was passionate in my beliefs to the point where that small event had a really big impact.
I was old enough to experience a deep feeling of betrayal but not old enough to view what happened in a wider context.
So in the face of racism I turned away and a chapter ended.
I wanted nothing more to do with religion whatsoever, and I turned away for a long long time.
Then there was just living my life.
College, English and comparative literature, getting married, having a good marriage at least for a while, Oliver and Nicholas, some of the world's greatest dogs.
I thought for a long time that you just lived your life as well as you could and there was no way to know what it really meant or what it really was about.
So you just throw a ball for your dogs, invite friends for dinner, work hard and don't forget to take a walk on the beach and smell the salt air.
I thought it wasn't really possible to understand what life was about, but it wasn't don't know mind of Dogen.
It was not just a beginner's mind.
I just was totally oblivious to what might be the meaning of our lives.
So it was mountains or mountains in terms of Dogen.
My husband wanted kids.
I wasn't so keen on the idea.
I had edited a book on medical ethics when I worked for a college textbook maker and it scared me.
In fact it scared the shit out of me, learning all the things that could go wrong.
I didn't want anything to do with having kids and I never really had a longing to have children anyway.
But Ford, my ex-husband, convinced me to take a leap of faith that this would be a great wonderful thing to do.
So we tried to have kids and couldn't get pregnant, so then we looked at adoption and we got Nathaniel when he was five days old.
He was a little tiny baby and his birth mother brought him to us.
We had a meeting with his birth mother, and then she was the one who left him with us.
I knew from previous things I've been exposed to that I didn't have any interest in taking on a special needs kid or a child who needed special care, and Nathaniel was fine.
But as Lieutenant O'Hara said once to Captain Kirk, be careful what you wish for.
You may get it.
And my mantra became, be careful what you wish not for.
You will get it.
When he was about nine months old the doctor was asking me, well, are you talking to him?
Do you do ma-ma-dada stuff?
Nathaniel wasn't making a sound.
He had a voice but he wasn't making any words or attempting to talk at all, and I did that all the time.
I talked to him constantly, and even to this day Nathaniel hears but he can't talk.
That's why I use sign language, not that he needs the sign language to understand me because he can hear, but to give him a way to communicate to other people.
I wanted him to learn signing.
Nathaniel also, well, he signs but not fluently.
He gets frustrated and bangs his head on the wall or on the floor.
They had to clear out the swimming pool at the, oh I forget what it's called, the Hanna whatever swimming pool.
They had to clear out the pool one time because Nathaniel banged his head on the edge of the concrete and bloodied his head, which got into the water.
It was probably a tablespoon of blood, but they had to clear out the pool.
That was pretty exciting.
So Nathaniel wants what he wants when he wants it.
He gets frustrated and makes it very clear when he's unhappy, and it was relatively easy to deal with that in a four-year-old.
It's actually much harder to deal with it in a 24-year-old.
But he can be really sweet too.
When I was teaching at Wellcome Community College I would bring students' papers home.
I taught writing classes a lot and I would bring students' papers home to work on them and mark them up, and I started noticing one time that some papers seemed to be disappearing.
It turned out that Nathaniel was taking some papers into his room and putting them in his bookcase.
So I eventually just made a stack of papers he was allowed to take from a certain place, so that he wouldn't take my students' papers and lose them.
And finally one day I asked him, why do you want mom's papers, and he said, love mom.
So he still says that sometimes.
He communicates by asking questions rather than making statements, so he will still ask me, why want mom's papers, and then I'll say, oh well why, Nathaniel, and he'll still say, love mom.

Last year Andrea gave a talk about a young woman whose child had died and she was charged by the Buddha, I think, with the task of finding a mustard seed from a family that had not suffered any kind of loss.
I sat here crying during the whole talk because it felt to me like, when a death happens, it's over but with a special needs kid you have multiple deaths, many, many times.
It's a kind of death when the child doesn't start talking.
It's a kind of death when he never wants to read or write.
And it doesn't end, so it's difficult, but turning away from me was not a choice.
I couldn't do that, but I was angry at the universe, and that's where the subject of our practice period comes from: anger, because I've been trying to deal with that for the last 17 years.
I was given this situation, I couldn't turn away, I had to find some way to embrace it, and it was the anger that brought me to practice.
My very first question of Norman and Doko-san was, "I'm here because I'm angry and I don't want to live my life in anger."
And I'm still here.
I read a couple of books: Stephen Batchelor's *Buddhism Without Beliefs*, which I highly recommend, and Charlotte Joko Beck's *Everyday Zen*.
Then I read 10 more books and I started coming to sit at the old dharma hall.
There were about five or six people who sat regularly at that time: Bob and Tim and Nancy and John and whoever else I'm leaving out.
I was this brand new person who knew nothing about Buddhism whatsoever, and I was really welcomed, so I continued coming to sit.
In fact I ended up getting a Buddhist name, Nyogen Seiku, which is energy source pure emptiness.
The energy source was because I kept wanting us to do more and more.
We even had a winter retreat.
Bob's Jukai was almost a disaster because we had a winter retreat at Sandwich Island and it snowed and it snowed and it snowed, and luckily everyone got home safely.
I had two Buddhas and an Amulokiteshvara in the car with me.
I've mentioned before that I was lucky when I came to the Introduction to Zen half-day retreat led by Norman.
I just knew I didn't need to look further.
When I'm choosing something, I always try to look at all the options that are possible before I make a decision or make a choice.
Once I heard Norman talk, the choice was made.
I didn't even look at any other possible meditation groups.
I just was part of Zen.
I'd found a teacher, but I didn't know yet that I had also found Buddha and Dharma and Sangha.
Tim can attest that when I first started with the group I beat myself up constantly whenever I'd make any kind of a mistake with the forms, especially if I was doing a job like Tengken or Doan.
You guys are lucky, the Doan and Kokyo books are in great shape.

At that time they were in their infancy and they weren't well marked up, and changes to procedures were likely to be on a post-it note from Tim given to me during Ken Hen right before the service, and I'd get very upset.
Apparently, well okay, we're up to about chapter seven at this point, apparently it's fairly common during someone's very first retreat to decide about day three that they're out of there.
This was in Samish Island in 2000.
I always remember the date because it's the year that Tim ordained, and it was my first retreat, and by Tuesday I was mentally done with it.
I would stay for the whole week because I had said I would, but I was done.
Then I got up early on Wednesday morning, of course, and sat down on a large rock overlooking the lagoon at Samish Island.

There were pink clouds reflected in the water, and about 80 great blue herons, I'm not exaggerating, about 80 great blue herons flew out of the north across the lagoon, going to wherever they were going for the morning, and my mind just stopped.
I don't know if it was 30 seconds, I don't know if it was two minutes, but for once I didn't have any mental chatter going on.
My mind was quiet, and I didn't leave the retreat, and I'm still here.
I realized when I was working on this talk just how much the way that I beat myself up about the forms and about Sangha paralleled the way I beat myself up in life.
Sometimes I did get a message of not being good enough from other people, but I also finally realized that that message was coming from deep within myself more than from other people.
When I started, I really loved the rituals.
I thought they were really beautiful but mysterious.

I could follow what others were doing and repeat the chants, and at first the rituals didn't mean a lot, but then I was participating more and sitting regularly, and through practicing over a long period of time the ritual seemed like it became a part of me.
I still just love the rituals of Zen.
Sometimes it becomes rote, but as Norman has pointed out, that just makes it all the better when it isn't.
It's not a thing that can be separated out from practice, so ritual and practice to me are the same thing.
Ritual is a process, it's empty, and it's truly transformative.
There's a koan, I think I have this right, that points to the nature of ritual.
A monk asks what is zazen, and someone, I think it might have been Zhaozhou, says non-zazen.
The monk asks how can zazen be non-zazen.
Zhaozhou replies, because it's alive.
So whether it's zazen or kinhin or offering flowers, the ritual to me is something that's really alive.
It creates sacred space, and for many years I could sit in that sacred space with tears running down my face and cry and let go.
I could face the grief that I couldn't face when I had to be fixing Nathaniel's dinner or dealing with one of his meltdowns or something else that was a problem, taking him to therapy, loving him.
But in that ritual space I could step back and look at all of that and be with it and feel it and find some peace with it.
It's still hard.
Most of you have probably heard that I take Nathaniel to a therapy band called Out of the Ashes.
Of course the people in the band, that's just the band, that has nothing to do with therapy, and he is excited when he gets there.
There's a drummer, I'm in love with this guy.
He comes and sets up a full drum kit and he plays for a while, and then he starts turning this full drum set over to these people with special needs.

So there are about four really good musicians and then the rest of the band is people with special needs, and Nathaniel will play the xylophone or the drums or guitar, or oh, he used to play piano, all kinds of things.
There are always instruments for people to pick out of a box and bang on something, so you can't go there and say, "Oh, but I can't play, I'm not musical."
So come sometime.
During the winter it's on Tuesday nights or Tuesday afternoons from three to five at the veterans hall down State Street, and somewhere it's a Boundary Bay, which is sort of more fun.
So Nathaniel plays in a rock band, and about a year ago he got to drive an enormous John Deere tractor.
I took him to the John Deere store just thinking I was going to get him a t-shirt or something, and I asked one of the salespeople if he knew of any way I could get Nathaniel a ride on a tractor.
Did he know of any owner who might be willing to give him a ride?
And the guy thought for a second and said, "We can do that."
So he went and got this absolutely enormous tractor, I wasn't as tall as the wheels on this tractor, and Nathaniel got to drive it.
The look on his face, just utter awe, was amazing.
It was incredible.
So, getting up to the current chapter, I have been having a lot of trouble with chronic pain that just doesn't go away.
It's pretty severe back pain, so I wake up in the night sometimes and listen to Dharma talks.
I love being, you know, that is one of the great jobs in the Sangha, being able to sit facing outward.
It gives you a feeling of caretaking: if the guy comes to the door with an Uzi, I'm the one who has to get up and tackle, because I'm the one who's facing outwards.
So keep that in mind.

And now I am shuso, and I'm still worried that I don't have enough energy to do the job well, but sometimes I can do what I did last year: get in the car on a sunny day and roll down the windows and put on some Fleetwood Mac and feel like I'm about 16.
I do feel like, as I'm getting older, I notice the beauty of the world more.
A tree trunk that I pass every day when I take my dog for a walk has green and purple and brown and all these different colors.
It's a cedar, I think, and I'm sure it's a cedar, and every time I see it it's just so incredibly beautiful.
How can this world be so beautiful and also such a hard, deadly place for so many people?
So sometimes I'm present, appreciating the sharp tangy ozone smell of saltwater or the green smell of that red cedar, or watching to see if hummingbirds are going to come back this year to my deck.
And sometimes, once in a great while, I experience a deep sense of peace, sort of the sound of silence, and maybe it's a slight brush with emptiness.
The one thing I really know is that I really don't know any of this.
I don't understand any of this, but that's okay.
So let me end with a quote from Norm Fisher.
He said:

*When we sit we recognize the crucial divine importance of absolutely everything that arises, every thought, every feeling, every breath, every unspeakable unnameable impulse, but we also recognize the ultimate importance of the others, of the sky, of all the sounds inside and outside the room.
As the mind becomes a little more quiet, the sacredness of everything within and without becomes clear to us.*
So I'll read that one more time:

*When we sit we recognize the crucial divine importance of absolutely everything that arises, every thought, every feeling, every breath, every unspeakable unnameable impulse, but we also recognize the ultimate importance of the others, of the sky, of all the sounds inside and outside the room.
As the mind becomes a little more quiet, the sacredness of everything within and without becomes clear to us.*
Respectfully submitted, Nyogen Connie Martin.
